summary: Defines a YANG data model for representing, retrieving and manipulating Traffic Engineering topologies. It is a base model that technology-specific TE topology models can extend.

plainLanguage.summary: Traffic engineering path computation works on a graph of the network. This RFC defines a common way to store that graph as a YANG data model, so that nodes, links, the points where links meet nodes, and the spare capacity on each link are described the same way everywhere. Standards for particular kinds of network add their own fields on top of it.

subtitle: A common YANG model for the graphs that traffic engineering path computation runs on, built to be extended by models for particular network technologies.

tldr.problem: Traffic engineered networks keep a database of their nodes, links and spare capacity, and path computation runs on the graph that database forms. There was no common, protocol-independent way to represent, retrieve and change that graph, and none for a version tailored to one client.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8795 defines the YANG module ietf-te-topology, which augments the network topology model of RFC 8345 with TE nodes, TE links, link and tunnel termination points, connectivity matrices, templates and information sources.
tldr.outcome: It is a base model: writers of models for WSON, OTN and Layer 3 are told to extend its containers rather than define their own. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and nothing in its metadata obsoletes or updates it.

facts.label: Template priority range
facts.value: 0 to 65535, a lower number means higher priority

today: RFC 8795 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2020, and the metadata for it lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says the module is designed for use with implementations that support the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342), and it ships a companion state module for implementations that do not.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
A Traffic Engineering Database (TED) holds all the traffic engineering information about all the TE nodes and TE links in a network. The RFC calls the TED an essential component of traffic-engineered systems based on MPLS-TE and GMPLS. A TE topology is the schematic arrangement of the TE nodes and TE links present in a given TED, and it forms the basis for a graph on which traffic engineering path computation algorithms run. One traffic engineered system can hold more than one TE topology.

RFC 8795 defines a YANG data model, described in RFC 7950, for representing, retrieving and manipulating TE topologies. The model holds technology-agnostic building blocks, and it is meant to be augmented by other, technology-specific TE topology models.

Section 1.3 of the RFC fixes the prefixes used for the imported modules, so that data node names are unambiguous: yang for ietf-yang-types, inet for ietf-inet-types, nw for ietf-network, nt for ietf-network-topology, and te-types for ietf-te-types.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic engineering needs a graph of the network before it can choose a route. RFC 8795 defines one common way to store and exchange that graph, so that different systems describe the same network in the same terms.

sections.title: The Elements of a TE Topology
sections.content:
A TE topology is a traffic engineering representation of one or more layers of network topologies, and it maps to a TE graph. The TE nodes are the vertices and the TE links are the edges.

A TE node represents one or several nodes, or a fraction of a node, which can be a switch or router that is physical or virtual. It belongs to and is fully defined in exactly one TE topology, and it is assigned a unique ID within that topology. A physical node that provides switching functions at several network layers can be decomposed into several logical TE nodes, each a fraction of the physical node, and those logical nodes may sit in the client-layer topology while the rest sit in the server-layer topology.

A TE link represents one or several physical links, or a fraction of a link. It also belongs to exactly one TE topology and has a unique ID within it. It attaches to a TE node and is terminated there by exactly one Link Termination Point (LTP), a conceptual point of connection between a TE node and one of the TE links it terminates. The cardinality between an LTP and its associated TE link is 1:0..1.

A Tunnel Termination Point (TTP) is hosted by exactly one TE node and represents one or several potential transport service termination points, such as a service client adaptation point such as a WDM/OCh transponder. It is assigned a unique ID within the scope of its node, and depending on the node's internal constraints a given TTP could be accessed via one, several, or all of the TE links terminated by that node.

Two lists then constrain what a path may do at a node:

  • The TE node connectivity matrix describes the node's switching limitations as the valid switching combinations of its LTPs. For a path arriving at the node on a given inbound LTP, the matrix names the outbound LTPs the path is permitted to leave by.
  • The TTP Local Link Connectivity List (LLCL) lists the TE links terminated by the node hosting a TTP, to which the TTP could be connected. For the path of a connection, the LLCL gives the valid TE links the path needs to start or stop on for the connection to terminate successfully on that TTP.

A TE path is an ordered list of TE links and/or TE nodes on the TE topology graph that interconnects a pair of TTPs. TE paths can be the product of a successful path computation performed for a given transport service.

In the RFC's Figure 1, the connectivity matrix on Node-2 is {<LTP-6, LTP-1>, <LTP-5, LTP-2>, <LTP-5, LTP-4>, <LTP-4, LTP-1>, <LTP-3, LTP-2>}, the LLCL on Node-1 is {<TTP-1, LTP-5>, <TTP-1, LTP-2>, <TTP-2, LTP-3>, <TTP-2, LTP-4>}, and the TE path for TE-Tunnel-1 is {Node-1:TTP-1, Link-12, Node-2, Link-23, Node-3:TTP-1}.
sections.plainLanguage: A TE topology is a graph of nodes and links. Each link ends at one named point on its node, and two lists say what a path may do: the connectivity matrix names the entry points that can reach which exit points, and the local link connectivity list names the links a service can start or end on.

sections.title: Layers, Transitional Links and Inter-layer Locks
sections.content:
Networks are typically built in several layers, where one or more signals in the client-layer network are multiplexed and encapsulated into a server-layer signal. The RFC gives two examples: IP over MPLS over Ethernet, and low-order Optical Data Unit-k signals multiplexed into a high-order ODUl signal carried over an Optical Channel signal in an Optical Transport Network.

Each layer on its own would be an isolated topology. To compute a path across the layers, the model adds the transitional TE link. It represents the layer transition function inside a node, the function that multiplexes and encapsulates client-layer signals into a server-layer signal, and that function is typically realised in hardware. A transitional TE link connects a client-layer node with a server-layer node. An ordinary TE link has LTPs of exactly the same kind at each link end, while the transitional TE link has client-layer LTPs on the client side and, in most cases, a single server-layer LTP on the server side.

Transitional links exist only while they are not in use, because they represent potential connectivity. Once a server-layer trail has been established between the server-layer LTPs of two transitional links, the resulting client-layer link in the data plane appears as an ordinary TE link in the client-layer topology. The transitional links reappear when the server-layer trail is torn down.

The TE inter-layer lock records how the layers adapt onto each other. It is an association of M client-layer LTPs with N server-layer TTPs, within which data arriving at any of the client-layer LTPs could be adopted onto any of the server-layer TTPs. It is identified by an inter-layer lock ID, unique across all the TE topologies the same provider offers, and the LTPs and TTPs in the group all carry that same ID as an attribute. A given LTP may have zero, one, or more inter-layer lock IDs, and a given TTP may have one or more. Each TTP also has an unreserved adaptation bandwidth attribute, which announces its remaining adaptation resources, sharable between all the potential client-layer LTPs.

Three further kinds of topology are built on that. An underlay TE topology is the base for constructing overlay topologies. An overlay TE topology is constructed based on one or more underlay topologies: each TE node of the overlay represents an arbitrary segment of an underlay topology, and each TE link of the overlay represents an arbitrary TE path in one of the underlay topologies. The overlay and its supporting underlays may describe different layer networks or the same one. An abstract TE topology contains abstract topological elements, and is an overlay topology created by a topology provider and customized for a client based on one or more of the provider's native topologies, the provider's policies and the client's preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks are built in layers, and traffic in one layer is often carried inside a signal in the layer below. The model adds a transitional link for the function inside a device that moves traffic between the layers. It stands in for a connection that does not exist yet: once a real trail is set up below, the upper layer sees an ordinary link instead. Inter-layer locks then record which points in the lower layer an upper-layer point may be adapted onto.

sections.title: Native, Customized and Merged Topologies
sections.content:
Native TE topologies. The model can represent and retrieve the native topology of a traffic engineered system. An implementation MAY construct one from all the nodes and links present in the TED, or construct separate topologies from what each information source reported, for example one from OSPF-TE and one from IS-IS-TE, or one per technology layer.

Customized TE topologies. A customized topology is one the provider has modified to honour a particular client's requirements or preferences. It typically makes abstractions on the provider's native topology, and it contains sufficient information for the client to compute and select paths according to its own policies. A customized topology is not necessarily an abstract one: a client may ask for a version with the TE links that belong to certain layers, are too slow, are not protected, or have a certain affinity removed, and the result is customized but contains no abstract elements. The client-id field in the topology identifier says which client the topology is customized for, and a client may customize only topologies whose client ID is 0 or matches its own. If the client starts reconfiguring a topology, its client ID is set automatically in the topology ID field for all future configurations and updates on that topology. By setting its own ID there, the provider MAY tell the client that the topology cannot be renegotiated. Implementations MAY restrict a particular client to particular data fields, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model provides such a mechanism.

Merging topologies from several providers. A client that receives topologies from several providers is expected to merge them into one or more of its own native topologies, each representing the multi-domain network uniformly, so that it can select end-to-end paths for services traversing several domains. The merge does three things:

  • It identifies neighbouring domains and locks their topologies together horizontally by connecting their inter-domain open-ended TE links.
  • It renames TE node IDs, link IDs and SRLG IDs into a namespace of its own, because the topologies are generally independent and their identifiers can clash.
  • It locks topologies of different layer networks together vertically, following the inter-layer locks the provider supplied.

To join neighbouring domains, an inter-domain TE link can carry the remote node ID and link ID. The RFC calls this less flexible, because the providers may not know each other's identifiers, and because it does not let a client mix and match more than one topology from the same provider. The more flexible option is the inter-domain plug ID, a network-wide unique number that identifies on the network the connection supporting a given inter-domain TE link. Two neighbouring topologies can each carry an open-ended inter-domain link with a matching plug ID, the RFC's example being 175344, and the client can then resolve the two links regardless of the node and link IDs, which may have been allocated from independent namespaces. Plug IDs may be assigned and managed by a central network authority, or discovered dynamically, for example with the Link Management Protocol.

Several abstract topologies from one provider. A provider may expose more than one abstract topology to a client, for example one optimised on a lowest-cost criterion, another on best possible delay, and another on maximum bandwidth availability. It is up to the client to decide how to mix and match them and how many merged native topologies to maintain. Each of the merged topologies could be used to compute paths for any of the multi-domain services, and the choice depends on the service parameters and requirements, on the topology's style and optimisation criteria, and on the level of detail. The RFC notes that allowing the client to mix and match assumes the inter-domain plug ID is used, rather than a remote node ID and link ID.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider can give a client its own network, or a version edited for that client, either by hiding detail or by removing links the client does not want. When a client collects versions from several providers, it joins them: it pairs the links that end at a neighbour's border, renumbers nodes and links so the identifiers do not clash, and records how the layers fit together.

sections.title: Model Structure and Topology Identifiers
sections.content:
The model is expressed as an augmentation. It extends the ietf-network-topology module defined in RFC 8345, and is itself written in YANG 1.1 as the module ietf-te-topology with the prefix tet and the revision date 2020-08-06. It imports ietf-yang-types, ietf-inet-types, the common traffic engineering types of RFC 8776, and the ietf-network and ietf-network-topology modules of RFC 8345.

Where it attaches to the network topology model:

  • A te-topology entry in the list of network types, marking a network as a TE topology.
  • A te container at the top of the networks list, holding the templates container with its node-template and link-template lists.
  • On each network, a te-topology-identifier container and a te container.
  • On each node, a te-node-id leaf and a te container with the node's te-node-attributes, its connectivity-matrices and the list of tunnel-termination-point entries with their local link connectivity.
  • On each link and each termination point, a te container, with a te-tp-id leaf on the termination point.

Topology identifiers. A TE topology is uniquely identified by a key of three constituents: topology-id, provider-id and client-id. The combination of provider ID and topology ID uniquely identifies a native TE topology on a given provider. The client ID is used only when customized topologies come into play, and a client ID of 0 is used for native topologies.

Generic link attributes. The model covers bandwidth, administrative groups, SRLGs, switching capabilities and TE metric extensions for a link: administrative status, link index, administrative group, link protection type, maximum link bandwidth, maximum reservable link bandwidth, unreserved bandwidth per priority, the TE default metric, and the SRLG and NSRLG lists. Bandwidth figures are in bytes per second, and the unreserved bandwidth list covers priority levels 0 to 7.

Generic node attributes. A node's te-node-attributes container holds its administrative status and its connectivity matrices. Each matrix entry has an ID, a from and a to termination point reference, an is-allowed flag that says whether switching is allowed, and the path attributes. The same shape is used for the local link connectivity entries under a tunnel termination point. Attributes placed directly under connectivity-matrices are the defaults for every entry, and a per-entry attribute overrides the corresponding default. The same rule applies to local-link-connectivities.

Each TTP MAY be supported by one or more supporting TTPs. If the TE node hosting the TTP refers to a supporting TE node, the supporting TTPs are hosted by that node; if it refers to an underlay TE topology, the supporting TTPs are hosted by one or more named TE nodes of that underlay topology.
sections.plainLanguage: The model adds traffic engineering fields to an existing network topology schema rather than replacing it. Every topology carries a three-part key: who provides it, which client it is for, and which topology it is. A client ID of zero means the provider's own topology. Each node then holds its own identifier, its connectivity matrix and the list of points where a service can terminate.

sections.title: Information Sources, Hierarchies and Templates
sections.content:
Information sources. Each TE topological element may have several information sources, and the RFC names OSPF-TE, IS-IS-TE, BGP-LS, user-configured and system-processed among them. Every source carries a credibility preference, which is the value used to break a tie between sources, and a higher value is preferable. The module's te-info-source enumeration lists the sources as unknown, locally configured, ospfv2, ospfv3, isis, bgp-ls, system-processed and other. When a customized topology is merged into a client's native topology, the merged topological elements point to the corresponding customized topology as their information source.

Overlay and underlay. The relationship between layers of topology is carried by the underlay-topology field on a node and the underlay field on a link. Both are optional and sit behind the te-topology-hierarchy feature, and they let a user start from an element in the topmost topology and traverse down to the supporting elements in the bottommost one. The link's underlay container records whether the underlay is enabled, names a primary path and any backup paths by index, and gives the protection type.

Templates. Users can define templates and apply them to link and node configurations. The feature is optional and tagged template. When two or more templates set the same configuration field, the value from the template with the highest priority is used. The priority runs from 0 to 65535, and a lower number indicates a higher priority. The reference-change-policy parameter says what happens when the template changes on a configuration element that refers to it: take no action, reject the change to the template, or apply the change to the corresponding configuration.

Scheduling. Time-scheduling parameters can be specified for each topological element or for the topology as a whole, so that a provider can present different topological views to the client in different time slots. Their use is optional, and the RFC relies on the separate YANG data model for configuration scheduling rather than changing its own model.

Notifications. The RFC relies on the subscription and push mechanisms of RFC 8639 and RFC 8641. With them a user can subscribe on a per-client basis, specify subtree filters or XPath filters so that only content of interest is sent, and ask for either periodic or on-demand notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Every element records where its data came from, such as OSPF-TE, IS-IS-TE or BGP-LS, together with a credibility value used to settle disputes between sources. Templates let an operator set the same attributes on many nodes and links at once; where two templates disagree, the one with the lower priority number wins, and the operator can decide what happens when a template is edited later.

sections.title: Writing Technology-Specific Augmentations
sections.content:
The base model is deliberately technology agnostic, holding the concepts, abstractions and attributes common to many network technologies. The RFC expects it to be widely used as the foundation for models of particular layer networks, and names models for WSON, OTN and Layer 3 as examples. Writers of such models are encouraged to augment the basic model's containers, for TE topologies, TE nodes, TE links, LTPs, TTPs, bandwidth and labels, with layer-specific attributes, instead of defining new containers.

Section 6 gives a worked example, the module example-topology. It adds an attributes container under the network's te container, under the node's te-node-attributes, under connectivity-matrices, under a connectivity matrix entry, under a tunnel termination point, under a termination point and under the link's te-link-attributes. It also adds a technology-specific case under the te-bandwidth and te-label choices in every place where those choices appear, in configuration data and in read-only data. The complete example module is given in Appendix C.
sections.plainLanguage: The base model is meant to be extended, not copied. An author writing a model for one kind of network adds their own fields inside the containers this RFC already defines, so tools that understand the base model can still read the extended one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines a schema for data that is designed to be accessed over network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, where the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH; the lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, where the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model provides the means to restrict a NETCONF or RESTCONF user to a preconfigured subset of all the available operations and content.

The writable data nodes are sensitive, and the RFC lists them together with what changing them can do. Modifying the te-topology network type can render the type invalid, and an attacker who does so may disable the TE capabilities on the related networks and cause traffic to be disrupted or misrouted. Modifying the templates changes the related future TE configurations. Modifying the network subtree, which specifies topology-wide configurations including the TE topology ID and topology-wide policies, can add, remove or modify TE topologies: adding one may create an unauthorized traffic network, and removing or modifying one may cause traffic to be disabled or misrouted in that topology, with effects that may also reach connected topologies. Modifying the node, link and termination point subtrees works in the same way at a smaller scale, and the effects can spread to surrounding elements and to connected topologies.

The readable data nodes are sensitive as well, so read access has to be controlled. Unauthorized reads can disclose the TE topology type, the node and link templates, the topology-wide configurations including the topology ID, the topology-wide policies and the topology geolocation, and the operational state of nodes, links and LTPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The model is meant to be reached over NETCONF or RESTCONF, and the RFC requires SSH or TLS underneath. It also lists what a careless change or an unwanted read would do, because both write access and read access have to be limited to the people who should have them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and the Companion Module
sections.content:
IANA registered two XML namespace URIs in the ns subregistry of the IETF XML Registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-te-topology and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-te-topology-state. It also registered two names in the YANG Module Names subregistry of the YANG Parameters registry: ietf-te-topology with the prefix tet, and ietf-te-topology-state with the prefix tet-s. Both entries reference RFC 8795.

Appendix B carries the second of those modules. The main module is designed for use with implementations that support the Network Management Datastore Architecture, but so that the model can still be used where that architecture is not supported, a companion module ietf-te-topology-state mirrors it as a state model in which every data node is non-configurable and represents applied configuration or derived operational state. The RFC calls this companion redundant, and says that implementations which do support the datastore architecture SHOULD NOT support it. Its tree is not drawn separately, because it mirrors the tree of the main module.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA recorded the two module names and their XML namespaces, so that nobody else can claim them. The RFC also ships a second, read-only module that mirrors the first, for equipment that cannot support the newer datastore architecture.

viz.caption: THE ELEMENTS OF A TE TOPOLOGY

items.title: TE node
items.text: A vertex. It can stand for one or several devices, or a fraction of one, and belongs to exactly one topology.

items.title: TE link
items.text: An edge. It can stand for one or several physical links, or a fraction of one.

items.title: LTP
items.text: The point at which a TE link is terminated by a TE node. Exactly one LTP terminates each link.

items.title: TTP
items.text: A point hosted by one TE node where a transport service can terminate.

items.title: Connectivity matrix
items.text: The valid switching combinations of a node's LTPs: which entry point can reach which exit point.

items.title: LLCL
items.text: The links a TTP could be connected to on the node that hosts it.

items.title: TE path
items.text: An ordered list of TE links and TE nodes that interconnects a pair of TTPs.
